newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian govt sees budget hope in Senate.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian govt sees budget hope in Senate.

text.p: Australian Government Senate Leader Robert Hill said the Australian Democrats' opposition to some budget measures did not mean those measures would be blocked in the upper house of parliament.

"As you know, on every bill in the Senate to get a majority we need a further two votes. We have options of the Labor Party, a Tasmanian Green -- I think he calls himself an Australian Green -- a Western Australian Green, Senator Harradine, Senator Colston and Australian Democrats," Hill said.
"So our objective is to garner two further votes to achieve our objective," he told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio.
On Wednesday, the Democrats, with seven senators, listed in a letter to Treasuer Peter Costello the budget measures they would oppose.
They said they opposed abolition of a dental benefits scheme, tightening of pharmaceutical benefits, higher court charges and higher university student charges.
Those measures need legislative authorisation and are therefore susceptible to blockage in the Senate.
But the Democrats also said they opposed cuts to the aboriginal welfare commission and the Australian Broadcasting Corporation, which they can do nothing about.

The Labor Opposition's treasury spokesman, Gareth Evans, said on August 21 that the overall shape of the budget would remain intact, although measures worth a few hundred million Australian dollars might be lost in the Senate.
The government's August 20 budget revealed measures saving the budget A$3.9 billion in the year to June 1997 and A$7.2 billion in 1997/98.
These measure are intended to produce an underlying budget surplus, that is, excluding asset sales, of about A$1 billion in 1998/99.
